title: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
headline: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

bullets.point: For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook.
bullets.detail: For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange. Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know.

title: Why the New Right is failing
headline: Why the New Right is failing

bullets.point: Art by Thomas Cole via Wikimedia Commons Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced…
bullets.detail: Art by Thomas Cole via Wikimedia Commons Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced by something we then called the “alt-right”. Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist. Over the course of two Trump presidencies and one Biden interregnum, the alt-right matured and grew into what I now call the New Right . In doing so, it basically took over from conservatism as the guiding ideology of the GOP base — though not (yet) of the GOP as a whole. Whereas the alt-right was a naked white-power movement, the New Right sees things in broader “civilizational” terms. It has embraced the idea of Christianity, not as a faith or a lifestyle, but as a tribal affiliation defining ingroup and outgroup. Its foreign policy matured into something concrete — a desire to wield American policy on behalf of “Western Civilization” . At the grassroots level, the New Right also added some new components. title: How artificial intelligence is offering new hope for stroke patients in the Last Frontier
headline: How artificial intelligence is offering new hope for stroke patients in the Last Frontier

bullets.point: It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime.
bullets.detail: It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime. On this summer Wednesday, a neurointerventionalist in Anchorage got the alert: Three hundred miles away, at a hospital deep in Alaska’s interior, a clot in a major artery was blocking the flow of blood to a patient’s brain. He needed it out — and he’d have to come to the state’s biggest city to get it done. Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots.

bullets.point: Time is never on a stroke patient’s side.
bullets.detail: Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots. In his mid-60s, the patient on the doctor’s phone had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. Like most patients with stroke symptoms, he got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke, whether it’s caused by a clot or a brain bleed, and determine whether that clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally, once the scan is complete, it could take 45 precious minutes just to send those thousands of two-dimensional brain snapshots to Anchorage for review — 90 million brain cells before a doctor could accept his transfer.

Her parents had declined a vitamin K injection for their baby, which is given to most newborns within six hours of birth to prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. With their baby on the verge of bleeding to death roughly 36 hours after birth, the parents agreed to let doctors administer vitamin K.

bullets.point: On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform.
bullets.detail: On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform. She had starved herself to death. Charlene had never been diagnosed with anorexia, not because her self-starvation went unnoticed, but because the diagnosis, in its Western form, was mostly unknown in the East. Her death changed that overnight. Splashed across the front pages were stark headlines such as ‘Girl Who Died In Street Was A Walking Skeleton’. Local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and quickly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it. The ideas spread rapidly – particularly that anorexia involved distorted self-perceptions about one’s body (dysmorphia) and an intense, borderline delusional, fear of gaining weight, often cued by prevailing beauty standards (notably, a cultural fixation with slender female bodies). Mass public education campaigns followed. Hotlines opened, celebrities spoke out. Anorexia became part of the zeitgeist.

bullets.detail: Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees. Most of these women did not obsess over their bodies, nor fear becoming fat. They instead complained of somatic (bodily) ailments: uncomfortable bloating, a profound lack of appetite. The cognitive hallmark of Western anorexia – a distorted body image – was largely absent. Lee seemed to be documenting a distinct form of self-starvation with its own local logic. The situation has changed dramatically since then. By 2007, more than three-quarters of the anorexic patients Lee treated cited ‘fat phobia’ as a central motivation. Today, anorexia in Hong Kong is terrifyingly common, affecting roughly one in 200 schoolgirls – comparable to trends in the United States. We do not know the form that Charlene’s illness took. What we do know is that her death became a catalyst for the rapid importation of a Western conceptual framework that reshaped how Hong Kong understood and experienced disordered eating in young women.

title: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart
headline: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart

bullets.point: Seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain.
bullets.detail: Seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain. It woke him up. It tingled down his arm. It ached along the whole length of his spine. A nurse working out of the operating room at a local hospital in Louisville, Colorado, Ruhling took an aspirin just to be safe. Surely , he thought, this is not a heart thing. He got up and rolled out his back. He didn’t think much of it. He went to sleep. The next morning, Ruhling pulled on his scrubs and went to work. The pain had not relented. He turned to one of the doctors on his floor and described the symptoms. The pain in his chest, the way it hurt when he bent over. At best, the doctor said, it’s nothing. At worst, he continued, you’re having an aortic dissection and you are about to die. Ruhling walked across the building and checked himself into his own hospital’s emergency room. headline: The Long Local History Behind Scott Colom

bullets.point: A few months ago, a retired newsman turned woodworker named Roger Larsen was busy refurbishing an old brick building that he owns in Columbus, Mississippi, when he saw his former…
bullets.detail: A few months ago, a retired newsman turned woodworker named Roger Larsen was busy refurbishing an old brick building that he owns in Columbus, Mississippi, when he saw his former neighbor Scott Colom filming an ad for his Democratic senatorial campaign on the steps of the county courthouse, across the street. Larsen is a conservative (“Alan Keyes was the last Presidential candidate I was excited about,” he said), but he admired the job that Colom had been doing as a district attorney for the past decade and said so. “I told him—of course, he wasn’t expected to win—I said, ‘When you win, Scott, I want you to have my building as your district headquarters.’ ” Larsen’s building is likely too small to be of practical use to Colom now that he has indeed won, becoming the state’s first Black senator-elect since Reconstruction. Just a couple of rooms, it was the Curly Top Beauty Shop for many years in the middle of the previous century. But it was originally built as a law office for James Thomas Harrison, a deputy to the Provisional Congress of the Confederate States. “Scott said that it would be symbolic,” Larsen recalled. Another attendee, arguably a bigger celebrity than the candidate himself, was Russ Hudson, a veteran of the war in Afghanistan who starred in the Colom campaign’s most viral ad, flipping burgers on a grill while drawling, “Shiiiiiiit, I’d rather pick another senator instead.” (Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, had answered a question about beef prices by saying, “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from.”) Still, another partygoer was George Irby, a revered longtime city employee who was drafted by the New York Giants, as a running back, in 1969, and then resettled in his native Columbus after his sports career. “I was amazed at the number of people, Black and white, that showed up,” Irby said. “Let me tell you, it goes beyond Columbus.
